articles.title: President Donald Trump Just Proclaimed, "Tariffs Don't Cause Inflation, They Cause Wealth," but Data From Federal Reserve Economists Show Otherwise
articles.summary: Statistically speaking, tariffs have been bad news for Wall Street and consumers.
articles.body:
From a purely statistical standpoint, Wall Street has enjoyed having President Donald Trump in the White House. Even accounting for a few periods of historic volatility (e.g., the COVID-19 crash in February-March 2020 and the tariff tantrum of April 2025), the average annual return of the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI), S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC), and Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) has been higher under Trump than under most presidents since the late 1890s.

However, this doesn't mean that all of the president's policies are necessarily well-received on Wall Street. For example, Trumpflation (inflation specifically driven by Donald Trump's policies) is a genuine threat to the artificial intelligence (AI)-driven bull market.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

President Trump's tariffs are doing more harm than good. Image source: Official White House Photo by Daniel Torok.

President Trump sees things differently. While speaking to an audience at a campaign rally in Montana ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Trump touched on inflation and the role his tariff and trade policy may have played in it. Said the president:

We don't have inflation, and tariffs don't cause inflation. You know what they cause? Wealth.

Although Trump insists that tariffs aren't contributing to persistently elevated inflation and are beneficial to the U.S. economy, reports from New York Federal Reserve economists show otherwise .

Tariffs have been foundational to Donald Trump's presidency

While tariffs have been a hot-button topic since Trump's second non-consecutive term began in January 2025, they've been a theme throughout both of his terms. In 2018, the Trump administration kicked off a trade war with China, imposing tariffs on washing machines, solar panels, steel, aluminum, and various tech goods.

President Trump's tariffs had three purposes:

To encourage overseas companies to manufacture their U.S.-bound products in America

To make U.S. products more price-competitive with those being imported

Shortly after the start of his second term, he introduced a new round of tariffs. Trump's April 2025 "Liberation Day" tariffs imposed a sweeping global duty and higher reciprocal tariffs on dozens of countries deemed to have adverse trade imbalances with America. A majority of these tariffs, imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, were invalidated by the U.S. Supreme Court in February 2026.

articles.title: Newsom amasses fundraising machine that could power 2028 bid
articles.summary: If California Gov. Gavin Newsom enters the 2028 presidential race, as many Democrats expect, he’ll walk in with an asset other White House hopefuls will inarguably envy: A small-dollar fundraising and organizing machine powered by a massive and ever-growing contact list of potential supporters across the country. Even before last year’s successful Proposition 50 redistricting…
articles.body:
If California Gov. Gavin Newsom enters the 2028 presidential race, as many Democrats expect, he’ll walk in with an asset other White House hopefuls will inarguably envy: A small-dollar fundraising and organizing machine powered by a massive and ever-growing contact list of potential supporters across the country.

Even before last year’s successful Proposition 50 redistricting effort in his state, Newsom had amassed more than 17 million email addresses, and his advisers say it’s only multiplied exponentially since then as Democrats feverishly donated in large numbers to redraw California’s electoral maps.

That list — advisers declined to provide its current size — has already helped Newsom raise more than $6.8 million during the midterm election cycle, Newsom’s advisers said. There have been more than 305,000 contributions this cycle, with $22.47 being the average donation, the advisers tell The Hill.

Newsom’s team said the bulk of the fundraising appeals have been funneled solely toward other Democratic candidates and causes. The governor, they say, remains hyper-focused on helping Democrats win in the midterms. Of the $6.8 million total, $1.85 million has been raised for 15 state Democratic parties, they said. And $2.2 million has been raised for Southern Democrats to help build infrastructure in the Deep South, which has been a sore spot recently for the party.

But should the governor launch a White House bid, the list would give him not only an automatic financial shot in the arm but a significant edge on outreach and organizing of potential supporters.

“Oh, of course, that’s a key advantage he’ll have in a presidential race,” said Garry South, a longtime Newsom ally who advised him in his first gubernatorial race. “First, any successful candidate in California starts out with a bigger donor base than anyone from another state because we’re the biggest state. But his national fundraising for Prop 50 provides him with a national fundraising base on top of his proven California donor list.”

Newsom has been building the list for years, dating back to 2021 when he was facing a recall. Back then, his list was relatively meager by comparison, with a quarter of million contacts.

By 2022, Politico reported that he had grown the list to 6 million and has supercharged it since, after he hired Tim Tagaris, who helped manage Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.)’s digital operation on his 2016 presidential campaign and helped turn Newsom’s list into its own potent political weapon.

In that time, the governor has reached out to supporters on a number of topics, including his various fights with Trump and Republicans on a series of fiery issues.

During the 2024 cycle, for example, Newsom had single-handedly poured more than $21 million into Democratic efforts and candidates with his small-dollar fundraising apparatus.

Other potential 2028 contenders including, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y), have also built powerful small-donor operations. Ocasio-Cortez, for example, raised more than $37 million during the current election cycle, with most of it coming from contributions of $200 or less.

At the end of September, her campaign reported more than $17 million cash on hand, giving her a strong foundation for what comes next. Ocasio-Cortez is weighing her next moves, including whether she’ll run for president or a New York Senate seat.

The way money plays in politics has changed over the years, and candidates like to show the electorate they’re not just relying on mega donors and super PACs to help win races.

“Money’s important but not determinative — just look at the literal billions the GOP is spending on midterm races, and still failing to close the gap,” said Democratic strategist Christy Setzer. “Money can buy name recognition but also a negative label from voters, who generally hate self-funders and the way money is so infused in our politics.

“A large amount of small dollar donations, however, are important as a show of strength and momentum; it’s a key reason AOC is mentioned in 2028 conversations,” Setzer said.

The appeals to the list are constant but targeted and intentional, Newsom allies say. In one missive in August, the governor sought support for two candidates in red states, former Rep. David Jolly in Florida and Jermaine Johnson in South Carolina.

“We’ve raised a lot of money for southern states and candidates running in southern states this year, and there’s a good reason for it,” Newsom said in one email. “These are places long-neglected by the Democratic Party.”

But he went on to explain in the email that “the only way back for those states is if we have the courage to fight — cycle after cycle — until we get it done.”

And Newsom’s team says the donations have made palpable changes — including in key states the governor would need to win in a 2028 presidential race. When he raised more than $579,000 for New Hampshire Democrats this cycle, part of that money helped fund a new Democratic field office in Nashua, along with support for state candidates down the line.

In South Carolina, the first state where Democrats will vote in the 2028 primaries, Newsom made some of his largest investments, his team said. His list helped raise more than $342,000 for the state’s Democratic Party; $53,000 for Johnson, the gubernatorial candidate; and more than $61,000 for six state House candidates.

Newsom’s team said that the legislative investments in South Carolina help telegraph his operation successfully: Candidates with small fundraising budgets can receive roughly $10,000 each, which is, in some cases, the entire budget of their campaigns.

In Nevada, another early state for Democrats, Newsom put the list to work to not only fundraise but build events in the state. When he appeared there with Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford — who is running for governor — and Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nev.) this summer, his team used the list to rally volunteers and open a new field office in the state.

And in his home state, on the heels of his successful Proposition 50 effort, Newsom directed half a million dollars for five congressional candidates running in districts made competitive by the redistricting initiative.

Newsom hasn’t yet decided if he will enter the race, even as many Democrats expect he will in fact wade into 2028 waters.

For now, his spokesman Izzy Gardon, said Newsom is “doing everything he can to help Democrats win” the midterms.

“He isn’t fundraising for himself,” Gardon said. “He is spending his time, his resources, and deploying his national small donor network to support candidates and parties who need the help — especially in down-ballot races that rarely get national attention.”

articles.title: Inflation under Trump is only about half the rate under Biden. Voters are still just as mad.
articles.summary: Prices in the US have risen only about half as fast in President Trump's second term compared to Biden's. Yet Trump risks paying a steep political price with...
articles.body:
So far in President Trump's second term, prices in the US have risen only about half as quickly compared to his predecessor's four years in office. Yet Trump has a 72% disapproval rating on the issue and risks paying a steep political price — just as former President Joe Biden did — with voters drawing a direct connection between rising prices and the president's policies.

In the last election cycle, prices of all items rose more than 20% during Biden's term , sparking widespread voter angst. This time around, price growth is notably slower, rising 5.4% in a little less than two years since Inauguration Day.

But a Yahoo Finance analysis of price data shows that a few major outliers have hit Americans' wallets in an outsized way, largely due to increases in goods affected by the war in Iran and tariffs.

Fuel oil and gasoline are perhaps the most dramatic examples, spiking over 30% beginning in March in response to the war in Iran and the closing of the Strait of Hormuz.

And voters have noticed, as evidenced in poll after poll. A New York Times/Siena poll released this week found 73% of likely voters disapprove of the president's handling of gas prices.

Trump underscored the salience of energy prices when he posted a charge this week that "Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the US Midterm Election."

Trump has often pushed back against questions about high energy prices, saying they won't be a problem once the Iran war ends.

Link between price spikes and Trump policies

The connection between price increases and Trump's tariff policy has also been in evidence.

Coffee prices have risen nearly 23% during Trump's second term (more than double the rate under Biden) as tariffs raised prices before Trump scrapped many of the coffee duties late last year in response to coffee drinkers' unhappiness.

Goods like toys and footwear have likewise risen rapidly as importers from China and elsewhere in Asia faced new tariffs. Toys are a particularly stark example, falling by 4.6% during Biden's term and then rising by 7.8% so far in Trump's term.

"Maybe the children will have two dolls instead of 30 dolls, and maybe the two dolls will cost a couple of bucks more than they would normally," Trump said in a rare acknowledgment of tariff-fueled price increases when he was pressed on the issue in April.

Other goods have moved in the opposite direction. Eggs jumped by an average of 2.57% each month when Biden was in the White House, but have dropped 3.82% each month of Trump's term so far, the analysis shows.

articles.title: Fake Social Security statement email hides a scam
articles.summary: A fake Social Security statement phishing email uses the SSA logo and a convincing layout, but the sender's domain instantly exposes the scam.
articles.body: There's something about an email from Social Security that makes you pay attention. After all, we're talking about your retirement benefits and years of earnings. So when a message lands in your inbox saying your statement is ready, clicking to take a look might seem perfectly reasonable. That's exactly what scammers are counting on. Take a look at this email below that recently landed in an inbox. It looks professional, carries the Social Security Administration (SSA) logo and includes a button to view a statement. However, a closer inspection reveals something the sender probably hoped you wouldn't notice. The message came from an email address with no apparent connection to the federal government. Even more concerning, the Social Security Administration's Office of the Inspector General warned in February 2026 about a significant increase in fraudulent emails using this same type of trick. Here's how to spot the warning signs in this email and protect yourself before scammers get their hands on your personal information. Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com. FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN How this fake Social Security statement email works The message arrives with the subject line "Statement Support Was Posted to Your Account Details Report." The sender appears as "Social Security Administrator," which immediately gives the impression of an official government communication. Inside, the email announces, "Your statement is ready." It goes on to say your 2025 Social Security statement is available and invites you to review your earnings record and benefit estimates online. There's even a neatly formatted box showing the year as 2025 and the status as "Ready." Below that sits a prominent blue "View statement" button. The message also displays what looks like the official Social Security website address. For someone quickly checking email before work or while getting through a crowded inbox, this could easily pass as a routine government notification. The sender's email address exposes the scam Here's where the message falls apart. Although the sender's display name says "Social Security Administrator," expanding the sender information reveals an address using the domain loradmiadministraciones.com . That's a major red flag. The address has no apparent relationship to Social Security, and the sender's domain does not end in .gov. Scammers can customize their display names to impersonate government agencies or other trusted organizations. According to the Social Security Administration, most legitimate SSA emails come from government email addresses. However, the agency does use some authorized outside services, including certain communications from echosign.com and approved marketing firms. That means you should examine the complete sender address and verify any unexpected request independently. Even a familiar-looking sender address can be spoofed. FAKE PATIENT PORTAL SCAM CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN AND INFECT YOUR PC Why the View statement button raises concerns The email encourages the recipient to click "View statement" to access what appears to be a routine financial document. That button is a central concern. A phishing link can redirect you to a fraudulent website designed to steal account credentials or sensitive personal information. Some malicious links can also lead to malware downloads. We haven't verified the destination behind the button in this particular email. However, the suspicious sender address and resemblance to known SSA phishing campaigns make the message unsafe to trust. The SSA's inspector general has specifically warned about fake statement notifications containing dangerous links. Those links could expose personal information or compromise devices. Why this Social Security scam looks so believable One interesting thing about this example is how little pressure it puts on the reader. There's no demand for immediate payment or warning that benefits will disappear within 24 hours. Instead, the message offers something people might genuinely want to see: their Social Security statement. It also uses the generic greeting "Dear Beneficiary," despite appearing in an inbox associated with a named recipient. That lack of personalization provides another reason to investigate, although generic greetings alone cannot prove an email is fraudulent. The professional appearance does much of the work. The SSA logo and government-style formatting create an impression of credibility. Yet none of those visual elements establishes who actually sent the email. Does Social Security really send statement emails? Yes, and that's what makes this scam particularly convincing. According to the SSA's official guidance, people with a personal my Social Security account generally receive an annual email reminder approximately three months before their birthday. The agency also sends certain notifications about new messages and notices. Scammers take advantage of these legitimate communications by creating messages that resemble official SSA reminders. How to check whether a Social Security email is legitimate Before opening a statement or following instructions in an unexpected email, take a few seconds to investigate the message. Check the sender's complete address On a computer, click the sender's name or expand the message details to reveal the full email address. On an iPhone or Android phone, tap the sender's name or address to view additional information. The exact method depends on your email app. Look closely at the domain. Watch for unfamiliar company names, extra characters or addresses unrelated to Social Security. Inspect the link without opening it On a computer, hover your mouse over a button or link without clicking. Your browser or email app may display its actual destination. On a phone, some email apps let you touch and hold a link to preview its address. Be careful because certain apps may open or begin loading a preview. When in doubt, skip this step and visit the official SSA website yourself. Remember that a website beginning with HTTPS can still be fraudulent. Encryption alone does not prove that a website belongs to the government. Verify the message directly with Social Security The most reliable approach is to open a new browser window and visit ssa.gov yourself. You can also contact Social Security at 1-800-772-1213 using the number published on its official website. Avoid using contact details provided in a suspicious email. How to safely access your Social Security statement You can check your earnings record and estimated retirement benefits without clicking an emailed statement link. If you don't already have an account, follow the official registration instructions. Creating an account can also help you monitor your Social Security information for unexpected activity. 7 ways to protect yourself from Social Security phishing scams A convincing email can catch anyone off guard, especially when it concerns retirement benefits or personal financial information. These practical steps can help protect your identity and accounts. 1. Be suspicious of unexpected statement links Even when an email looks authentic, use the SSA website independently to access your information. Avoid downloading unsolicited statement attachments or documents that claim to come from the agency. 2. Protect your account with strong authentication Use a unique password for your Login.gov or ID.me account and keep multifactor authentication enabled. Also protect the email account associated with your Social Security profile because criminals may target it to reset other passwords. 3. Use strong antivirus software Strong antivirus software can help identify dangerous websites and block known malware downloads. Keep your operating system, browser and security software updated to protect against newly discovered threats. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com 4. Be careful with your Social Security number Never provide your Social Security number or financial account information through an unexpected email link. If someone claims to represent Social Security and requests sensitive details, contact the agency through its official website. 5. Monitor your Social Security information Review your earnings history periodically through your personal SSA account. Look for unfamiliar earnings or changes to account details. If you notice something suspicious, contact Social Security directly for assistance. 6. Reduce the personal information scammers can access Scammers can collect personal details from people-search websites and data brokers to make their messages more convincing. Consider removing your information from these websites or using a reputable data removal service to handle supported requests. Although this won't stop every phishing attempt, it can limit some of the personal details criminals find online. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com 7. Report suspicious emails before deleting them The SSA Office of the Inspector General accepts reports of Social Security impersonation scams at oig.ssa.gov/report/ . Save the suspicious sender address and relevant screenshots. You can also report the message through your email provider's built-in phishing-reporting feature. Once you've preserved the information needed for a report, delete the email. What to do if you clicked a fake Social Security statement link Your next steps depend on what happened after you clicked. Here's how to respond. Clicked the link but didn't share information Close the suspicious website immediately. Avoid interacting with additional prompts or downloading files. If the site attempted a download, check your device's Downloads folder without opening the file. Simply visiting a phishing page does not automatically mean your information was stolen. However, keep your browser and operating system updated, and run a security scan with strong antivirus software if you notice anything unusual. Entered your password on a suspicious website Change the affected password immediately through the legitimate website, preferably using a trusted device. If you reused the password anywhere else, change it on those accounts too. A reputable password manager can help you create strong, unique passwords for each account and alert you to passwords that may have been exposed in a data breach. Next, review account activity and recovery settings. Check for unfamiliar sign-ins or unauthorized changes. Contact Login.gov, ID.me or the affected service through its official support channels if you believe someone accessed your account. Shared your Social Security number Visit IdentityTheft.gov for a personalized recovery plan. Consider placing a free credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. This can help prevent criminals from opening new credit accounts using your information. You should also review your credit reports and monitor financial accounts for unauthorized activity. Downloaded or opened a suspicious file Avoid opening the downloaded file if you haven't already. If you ran it, disconnect the affected device from the internet and perform a scan with strong antivirus software. If you suspect malware installed successfully, use a separate trusted device to change sensitive passwords. Consider getting professional assistance before signing back into financial accounts on the affected computer. Exposed financial details or lost money Contact your bank or financial institution immediately. Explain what happened and ask about securing your accounts or disputing unauthorized transactions. You should also report the incident to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov/ and the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov/ . The SSA's inspector general recommends these reporting channels for victims of Social Security impersonation scams. If you experienced financial loss, consider filing a report with local law enforcement. Kurt's key takeaways What concerns me about this particular scam is how routine the email feels. There are no dramatic threats or wild promises. It simply tells you that your Social Security statement is available, something millions of Americans have a legitimate reason to check. And the design is convincing enough that someone could click before thinking twice. I've said it before, and I'll keep saying it: A polished email doesn't tell you anything about who's really behind it. In this example, checking the sender's actual address exposed a serious warning sign immediately. My advice is simple. When an email involves your Social Security information, go directly to the government website and check for yourself. A few extra seconds of caution could save you from a much bigger headache. articles.title: Will the Fed drop any hints on rate rises?
articles.summary: Despite this week's rally in US Treasuries, investors fear the recent global bond sell-off is far from over, with traders looking to the Federal...
articles.body:
Despite this week's rally in US Treasuries, investors fear the recent global bond sell-off is far from over, with traders looking to the Federal Reserve's policy meeting and press conference on Wednesday for clues about the path of interest rates.

Traders in futures markets are pricing just a 9 per cent chance of a rate rise at the October meeting but anticipate between two and three quarter-point rises by the end of 2027, according to LSEG data.

Although US inflation came in higher than expected in September, many investors believe raising interest rates would do little to curb price pressures driven by soaring energy costs.

"We don't think they're going to raise rates," said Rob Waldner, chief investment officer at Invesco Fixed Income.

"There's no real inflation problem. There's a price problem in commodities and oil, but raising Fed rates doesn't solve the Iran war. It doesn't create more oil. It doesn't solve the diesel problem with refineries," he added.

The lack of forward guidance from new Fed chair Kevin Warsh is also expected to fuel volatility in the Treasury market, as investors struggle to gauge the central bank's next moves. Meanwhile, concerns over US government spending have kept longer-term borrowing costs elevated.

"We've introduced more risk premium and more volatility to the market," Waldner said. "We think the yield curve will steepen, and you'll probably get more risk premium on the long end of the curve." Michelle Chan

How close is the ECB to taking action on France?

The European Central Bank's October decision on interest rates is the part that is least in doubt before Thursday's meeting of the governing council.

Traders and analysts take it almost for granted that policymakers will leave the deposit rate unchanged at 2.5 per cent after raising it by a quarter point in June and again in September. LSEG data shows that markets are pricing just a 9 per cent probability of a rate rise next week.

Harder to predict will be any indication of the ECB's view on the situation in France, where 10-year government bond yields have risen above 5 per cent, the highest in more than two decades and some 1.7 percentage points above Germany's.

ECB watchers are pondering two questions. Will the rise in market rates delay further rises in policy rates, given that inflation is still on an upward trajectory? And how close is the ECB to buying French bonds to calm down the turmoil?

Traders on swaps markets have dialled down their bets on another quarter-point interest rate move this year, which was fully priced earlier this month, to about a 66 per cent chance.

articles.title: Trump Says Decision Time Nears on Iran: Deal or ‘Finish It Off’
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said it’s “getting to be decision time” on whether he will make a deal with Tehran or resume attacks as Iranian and Houthi threats aga...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump said it's "getting to be decision time" on whether he will make a deal with Tehran or resume attacks as Iranian and Houthi threats against Americans in the Middle East continue to grow.

"I have a decision to make: Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal? That's all," Trump said in an interview with Fox News' Sunday Morning Futures. "We don't play games."

Trump has suggested that US strikes on Iran could resume after the Nov. 3 midterm elections and he has sent additional forces, including a third aircraft carrier group, toward the Persian Gulf.

Officials warn the period between the election and the new Congress taking office could be particularly dangerous, with a negotiated deal seen as the most likely way to end the conflict.

The US is reducing diplomatic and military staffing in parts of the Middle East amid growing threats from Iran and the Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen.

The State Department had initially acknowledged departures only from Saudi Arabia, but an American official told Bloomberg News Friday that staffing changes are taking place more broadly as Iran intensifies attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Warsh Tells Traders to Watch the Data. They Still Follow the Fed
articles.summary: Early on Oct. 14, just hours before the release of a much-anticipated report on US inflation, TD Securities’ Gennadiy Goldberg recommended that clients bet a...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Early on Oct. 14, just hours before the release of a much-anticipated report on US inflation, TD Securities' Gennadiy Goldberg recommended that clients bet against a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike later in the month. The logic was that inflation would likely be benign enough to justify a hold. Equally important, a slew of Fed officials had spent days pushing back against expectations for an imminent move.

Then the data came in hot. Traders quickly ramped up bets on an October hike, at one point putting the odds at roughly 50-50, up from about 20% before the report — and Goldberg and his team began debating whether to abandon their brand-new trade. But almost as quickly as the market moved against them, it started swinging back. By the end of the day, most of that move had been erased. "We didn't even have a chance to take the trade off," said Goldberg, head of US interest-rate strategy.

Several market cross-currents were at play that day to stoke the roundtrip, including a stock selloff, AI jitters and increasing tensions in France. For many, though, it came down to the stream of Fedspeak signaling a pause in October. The seemingly explicit language stood out at a time when Chairman Kevin Warsh has said he wants to wean markets off such "forward guidance."

Caught in the middle, traders fell back on the familiar and took their cue from what policymakers were saying. But they also acknowledge that on its own, the inflation data might have spurred them to wager on an October hike. All of this leaves investors in a precarious position heading into this week's policy meeting, still somewhat guessing and prone to a jolt if their read of the situation turns out to be wrong.

"There's a disconnect between what Warsh has said and what the others have signaled," said Neil Dutta, head of economics at Renaissance Macro Research. "When you have this sort of development or condition, there's always a risk that the market can get whipsawed at any given meeting."

To be sure, recent market developments make the chance of such a whipsaw less likely. With AI shares continuing to slide and concerns starting to build around US growth prospects should the artificial intelligence boom falter, traders now have even less conviction that the Fed will raise rates next week — or even this year. Odds of an October move now stand at less than 15%, based on interest-rate swaps. But it was a different picture just a few weeks ago, when the series of speeches began.

articles.title: The 3 approaches to daylight saving time considered this year, and what happened to them
articles.summary: There were three possible approaches the U.S. could have taken this year regarding seasonal time change. Instead, our clocks will fall back as usual next month.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – In just a week, our clocks will fall back an hour as daylight saving time comes to an end. With it will come early sunrises and sunsets, and potentially some health benefits .

If some lawmakers had their way, however, the seasonal time change could have looked a lot differently this fall.

The U.S. nearly locked its clocks on permanent daylight saving time after the House passed the Sunshine Protection Act, sending it off to the Senate with support from President Trump. But the Senate adjourned without taking any action and isn’t expected back until after Election Day. (The legislation doesn’t have a “clear path forward,” though, according to Senate Majority Leader John Thune.)

Had the legislation taken effect, daylight saving time could have become permanent this year, and most U.S. clocks — Hawaii and most of Arizona are already on permanent standard time — would not be falling back in November. Several of our Canadian neighbors enacted permanent daylight saving time this year and will not set their clocks back next weekend.

The U.S. could have taken a different approach that would have set the clocks back an hour in November, as usual, but left them there permanently.

In July, the bipartisan “Sunshine for Our Kids Act” was introduced in the House. The bill calls for year-round standard time in the U.S. , though it would allow states the option to make daylight saving time permanent, an option not currently available to them without action by Congress.

If standard time were to become permanent, our clocks would not “spring forward” an hour in March. Our winters would feel as they do now, but the sun would rise and set an hour earlier than it currently does in spring, summer, and early fall.

The Sunshine for Our Kids Act was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce in July and remains there as of late October.

A third, less common approach to seasonal time change was also suggested this year: “half-daylight saving time.”

Under the Daylight Act of 2026, introduced in the House in February, our clocks would, essentially, fall back 30 minutes in November rather than a full 60 minutes. (If it took effect before March, clocks would spring forward 30 minutes instead of a full 60.) The twice-a-year changing of the clocks would also cease.

While it would be much less drastic than changing by an hour, you would likely notice a difference . Not only would sunrises and sunsets shift , but any international interactions — business, flights, or even crossing the Canadian border while visiting Niagara Falls — would have to account for unusual time zones .

That bill was similarly referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, where it remains as of October.

Also introduced in Congress were two bills that would give states the option to observe year-round daylight saving time, action nearly 20 states have been awaiting . Neither bill progressed out of committee.

For now, our clocks will fall back on the earliest possible date , Nov. 1.

articles.title: Schiff: Hegseth should face Senate questions over Starlink slowdown
articles.summary: Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) on Sunday called for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to testify before the Senate over Starlink’s slowdown to its satellite service in Ukraine, which disrupted the country’s military capabilities. On NBC News’s “Meet the Press,” Schiff told host Kristen Welker that if Democrats were to regain control of the Senate, Hegseth “should…
articles.body:
Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) on Sunday called for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to testify before the Senate over Starlink’s slowdown to its satellite service in Ukraine, which disrupted the country’s military capabilities.

On NBC News’s “Meet the Press,” Schiff told host Kristen Welker that if Democrats were to regain control of the Senate, Hegseth “should be brought in,” along with “anyone who has knowledge of what happened.”

The lawmaker pointed to conflicting accounts from President Trump and billionaire Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX operates Starlink, over who was responsible for limiting the service. The Wall Street Journal reported last week that Musk ordered the slowdown of Starshield, the military version of Starlink.

Musk on Saturday alluded to being behind the slowdown of Starshield, the military version of Starlink.

“Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” Musk said in a post on social platform X.

Musk also said that limits on “speed or usage” of the service were at the discretion of “the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS,” referencing the president of the United States.

“You’ve got the president saying one thing, you’ve got Elon Musk saying another thing, you have them both saying different things at different times,” Schiff said. “Somebody is lying here. Maybe they’re all lying in different ways, but we need to find out.”

Schiff argued that it raised broader questions about Musk’s influence over U.S. national security.

“The world’s richest person shouldn’t be controlling our national security interests,” he said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told NBC News last week that his government believed the U.S. had directed SpaceX to limit satellite speeds. The slow down targeted Starlink-supported Ukrainian military drones, airplanes and helicopters traveling faster than 100 mph, a source familiar with the matter previously told The Hill.

“It was the message from American government to limit this speed, and technically SpaceX did it,” Zelensky said.

The Trump administration has denied ordering the restrictions. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also shut down reports that Washington had denied Ukraine access to satellite services needed for its defense.

articles.title: Zen Browser is the Arc replacement I was looking for
articles.summary: Zen Browser rips off all the best bits of Arc without the AI and feature bloat, making it the perfect replacement.
articles.body: I know many of you are mourning the loss of the Arc browser, and I get it. It felt like the first app in a long time to really offer a new approach to browser design. Atlassian bought the company last year and shifted its focus to developing Dia, its even more AI-focused browser. And soon enough, Arc will officially be no more, leaving dedicated users in a lurch. But I abandoned Arc quite some time ago for the Zen Browser and haven’t really missed it. If you’re willing to deal with some minor inconveniences, I think you’ll find Zen is the Arc replacement you’re looking for. Zen unabashedly rips off all the best bits of Arc. Visually, they’re almost indistinguishable. It has the launcher-like pinned sites, tab bar on the left, siloed spaces, and mods that let you customize the browser’s UI to your liking. It takes the bits that made Arc’s interface feel fresh, then strips out everything that made it bloated and drove me into the arms of another. Most notably, Zen is AI-free. There’s no agent in a sidebar hounding me to let it handle tasks. I’m not worried about Zen training an LLM on my browsing activity. It’s just a web browser. Zen prides itself on its privacy features: “Beautifully designed, privacy-focused, and packed with features. We care about your experience, not your data,” it proudly proclaims. Now, I’m no fool. I know that nothing I do on the internet is really private, but with Arc, it always felt like my data was an integral part of the business plan. That’s not the case with Zen. It’s a free and open-source project that relies on volunteers and donations. In addition to Zen Mods that can do anything from tweak the look of an active tab to overhaul how PiP videos are handled, you can also install Firefox extensions. Yes, you can install Chrome extensions in Arc, but anecdotally, I’ve found that Zen handles extensions better. Both Zen and Arc are different enough from a UI perspective that not all extensions display properly, but Zen offers more workarounds. Zen also just kind of lets me focus on the task at hand. Links open in “glance” view, which is a temporary pop-over tab, which is really great when you’re doing some window shopping or light research. If I want to open it in a proper tab, it’s just a click away. Zen also has a floating bar that pops up whenever you press Command+T or CTRL+T. From here you can launch a new tab, switch to an existing tab, perform a search from the search engine of your choice, and even trigger an extension. Zen isn’t perfect. I love its clean UI and organizational features, but it can’t play DRM-protected video content right now. That means Netflix, Spotify, HBO, Disney+, and more do not work in Zen. The Zen Team is working to obtain a Widevine license from Google. In the meantime, I use Chrome when I want to watch a movie, which is fine. Zen is built on Firefox, and Firefox’s Web MIDI support is lacking. So I have to fire up Chrome semi-regularly anyway. I also miss Arc’s Boosts in some cases, but I’ve learned to accept the web as it is. Zen implemented a similar Boost feature in May, but it’s not super obvious and, if there is an official, easily browsable repository of installable Boosts, I’ve yet to find it. Instead, you have to tweak individual sites’ appearance yourself. If you tried Zen a long time ago and were turned off by its buggy early builds, rest assured it’s come a long way. Look, if you are all in on Arc’s AI features, Dia is probably more your speed. Personally, I always loved Arc’s interface, but never really dug the vibes. Zen just feels right. Update October 25th: Added information about Zen’s implementation of Boosts.

articles.title: Crow: Elon Musk having control to cut off Starlink to Ukraine is ‘beyond disturbing to me’
articles.summary: Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.) on Sunday said that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk having the ability to cut off Starlink access to Ukraine is “beyond disturbing to me.” “Face the Nation” host Margaret Brennan asked Crow about satellite services provided by SpaceX being fully restored in Ukraine after Musk on Saturday alluded that he slowed down…
articles.body:
Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.) on Sunday said that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk having the ability to cut off Starlink access to Ukraine is “beyond disturbing to me.”

“Face the Nation” host Margaret Brennan asked Crow about satellite services provided by SpaceX being fully restored in Ukraine after Musk on Saturday alluded that he slowed down Starlink’s use for the Ukrainian military.

She asked if an “unelected official can have such unilateral influence over our national security policy?”

“Yeah, it appears to be the case, and it’s beyond disturbing to me, which is why I also wrote a letter directly to President Trump, along with Adam Smith of the Armed Services Committee and Jim Himes of the Intelligence Committee … saying we deserve answers,” Crow said.

“It cannot and should not be the case that a tech oligarch, a private citizen, who has the most control over our national security, who is unaccountable, who is unelected, with zero transparency, is making life-and-death decisions on the battlefield, and systems that our service members and our partners and allies rely upon,” he added. “It should not be the case.”

Crow said the Trump administration allowed this to happen and vowed that Democrats will “try to stop it.”

Musk wrote on his social platform X that Starlink was slowed down because the “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people.” He added this “loophole” was closed last week.

This slowdown happened as the Ukrainian military faced restricted access to Starshield, the military version of Starlink, which affected military drones, airplanes and helicopters traveling more than 100 mph. Musk maintained that the U.S. government controls Starshield and that what “they decide to do is up to them.”

“Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” Musk wrote Saturday.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Saturday that satellite links had been restored and thanked “all Americans” and partners who assisted in this effort, including U.S. lawmakers, the State Department, the media and Trump.

After The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk ordered the slowdown of Starshield, several Democrats called for an investigation into the matter.

Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) told NBC News’s “Meet the Press” that, should Democrats regain control of the Senate, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should testify about what happened with the slowdown.

Trump has denied ordering any restrictions on Starlink’s usage in Ukraine.

“You’ve got the president saying one thing, you’ve got Elon Musk saying another thing, you have them both saying different things at different times,” Schiff said. “Somebody is lying here. Maybe they’re all lying in different ways, but we need to find out.”

articles.title: Republicans struggle for an answer to Democrats’ Medicaid attacks
articles.summary: Democrats across battleground districts are holding Republicans’ feet to the fire over the Medicaid cuts in their signature One Big Beautiful Bill law. In advertisements and on debate stages, the Democrats are hammering their opponents over their support for a law that will reduce Medicaid funding by nearly $1 trillion to pay for tax cuts primarily…
articles.body:
Democrats across battleground districts are holding Republicans’ feet to the fire over the Medicaid cuts in their signature One Big Beautiful Bill law.

In advertisements and on debate stages, the Democrats are hammering their opponents over their support for a law that will reduce Medicaid funding by nearly $1 trillion to pay for tax cuts primarily for wealthy individuals and corporations.

With less than two weeks before the midterm elections, Republicans are playing defense.

The Trump administration is focusing on fraud, suspending billions of dollars in Medicaid money to states and disenrolling hundreds of thousands of people from ObamaCare.

Some lawmakers are talking about smaller investments made as part of the law’s $50 billion rural health fund.

California Rep. David Valadao (R), who is running for reelection in a district with one of the highest Medicaid populations nationwide, defended his vote for the law.

“There are no actual cuts” to Medicaid, he said during a recent debate.

Valadao said the law preserved Medicaid for eligible groups and included additional funding for rural healthcare.

Last week, Maine Sen. Susan Collins (R) aired an advertisement about how she secured $190 million for her state’s rural hospitals — “the biggest federal investment in rural healthcare in more than 20 years.”

Collins voted to advance the legislation to the floor and was a key negotiator in securing $50 billion for the law’s rural health transformation fund. She ultimately voted against final passage, joining fellow Republican Sens. Thom Tillis (N.C.) and Rand Paul (Ky.).

During a heated debate against Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, Collins noted she had been able to secure funding for Maine’s rural healthcare in the law, which wouldn’t have been possible if she killed it in committee.

Jackson said Collins secured a “pittance” compared to the overall cuts in the law.

“Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who helped set the fire, and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” Jackson said.

The rural health fund will ultimately give Maine $950 million, and only a small percentage can be used to directly pay providers. The One Big Beautiful Bill will cut more than $2.5 billion from the state, according to an analysis from KFF.

During a debate last month in a toss-up district in Arizona, Democrat JoAnna Mendoza used similar language to attack incumbent Rep. Juan Ciscomani (R) for his vote in favor of the bill.

“It’s like bringing a glass of water to a fire that you started,” Mendoza said.

Ciscomani said the cuts would have been larger had he not pushed back.

Ciscomani was among 15 House GOP moderates who told leadership they couldn’t support legislation with deep cuts to Medicaid that would threaten hospitals. He voted for the bill anyway.

“Had we done the FMAP [Federal Medical Assistance Percentage] changes that were proposed initially on this bill, then the entire expansion population of Medicaid would have been off the books,” Ciscomani said during the debate. “That would have been devastating for the state.”

Arizona received $167 million from the first tranche of the rural health fund this year; the One Big Beautiful Bill is projected to cut $34.5 billion from the state.

Polling over the past year has consistently shown that voters are worried about the cost of healthcare and trust Democrats more to fix it.

A survey from KFF earlier this month showed voters overall trust Democrats to handle healthcare costs by a nearly 2-to-1 margin over Republicans.

A Gallup survey from March found more Americans were concerned about the “availability and affordability of healthcare” more than any other domestic policy issue, and one-third made at least one tradeoff of daily living expenses to afford care.

According to data analyzed by the Cook Political Report and AdImpact, Democrats are also outspending Republicans on healthcare-focused ads; $70 million spent in House competitive races, and $96.5 million spent on competitive Senate races. Republicans have spent just under $68 million on healthcare in Senate races, and under $43 million in House races.

The One Big Beautiful Bill law is expected to reduce Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion through 2034, with the bulk of the cuts coming from a strict national work requirement on low-income childless adults, as well as new restrictions on state-levied taxes on health providers.

GOP strategists admit there isn’t a strong defense for Republican candidates if the Democratic attacks resonate.

Jason Cabel Roe, a Michigan-based Republican strategist working on Rep. Tom Barrett’s (R-Mich.) campaign, said Democrats are successfully warping the message about Medicaid.

“It is being portrayed as us, Republicans, cutting Medicaid as opposed to rooting out waste, fraud, abuse. Getting able-bodied people to have some minimum work requirements,” Roe said.

Roe said Democrats have been campaigning on “doom and gloom” about healthcare for decades.

“I think for a lot of voters, they just kind of tune it out,” Roe said. “Now, if you’re feeling the cuts, then that’s different.”

Chuck Coughlin, a Republican-turned-independent strategist in Arizona, said Republicans are being hammered no matter what they say.

Healthcare and Medicaid are part of the reason, but there are so many issues voters are angry about — like gas and food prices, tariffs and the war in Iran.
